ad1_phrase.topic: Origins of the phrase 'American Dream' and its roots

claims.text: James Truslow Adams popularised 'the American dream' in The Epic of America (1931), describing 'that dream of a land in which life should be better and richer and fuller for every man' and saying 'It is not a dream of motor cars and high wages merely' but of being able to grow to fullest development as man and woman (pp. 415-416).
Adams called the dream 'the dominant motif in the American epic' and 'a moving force as truly as wheat or gold' (p. 174).

Adams would have called the book The American Dream if his publishers had let him; it was a bestseller in one of the worst Depression years; Adams also wrote of 'a better, richer, and happier life for all our citizens of every rank'.
Adams (1878-1949) won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for History; he had been an investment banker and partner in a NYSE member firm before leaving finance for writing in 1912.
Lincoln, 4 July 1861: the Union fought for a government 'whose leading object is to elevate the condition of men', 'to afford all an unfettered start and a fair chance in the race of life'.

Lincoln, 30 September 1859: 'The prudent, penniless beginner in the world, labors for wages awhile', saves to buy tools or land, works on his own account, then hires another; 'If any continue through life in the condition of the hired laborer, it is not the fault of the system' but of dependent nature, improvidence, folly or singular misfortune.
Horatio Alger (1832-1899) wrote more than a hundred books selling over 20 million copies; Ragged Dick serialized 1867, book 1868; honest hardworking boys rewarded, usually through luck.

In Ragged Dick the hero rises after rescuing a drowning child whose grateful father gives him a job; he ends as a respectable middle-class clerk, not rich; Carl Bode and Gary Scharnhorst read Alger as 'rags to respectability'.
Churchwell (2018): 'the American dream' initially represented a broad vision of democratic and economic equality, and was entangled from the 1910s with 'America First'.

ad1_taught.topic: How the Dream is taught: standards, textbooks, civics test, pop civics, and belief

claims.text: Declaration of Independence (1776): unalienable rights including Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.

CEE Standard 13: 'Income for most people is determined by the market value of the productive resources they sell. What workers earn primarily depends on the market value of what they produce.' Standard 15: investment in factories, machinery, new technology, and in the health, education and training of people stimulates growth and can raise future standards of living.
C3 D2.Eco.13.9-12: explain why investments in capital goods and human capital increase economic growth and standards of living.

AP US History CED Topic 8.4: KC-8.3.I.A 'A burgeoning private sector, federal spending, the baby boom, and technological developments helped spur economic growth'; KC-8.3.I.B increasing social mobility encouraged migration of the middle class to the suburbs.

Texas high school economics course is titled 'Economics with Emphasis on the Free Enterprise System and Its Benefits' (§118.4, adopted 2010); students explain 'the benefits of the U.S. free enterprise system'.
Texas SBOE approved the economics standards 14-0 in May 2010; the course name dates from 1997 and comes from the Texas Education Code.
As of 22 October 2026, 30 states guarantee a personal finance course before high school graduation (11 fully implemented, 19 in progress), up from 17 in 2022.
Mankiw's eighth principle: the standard of living depends on a country's production.
Schoolhouse Rock! began airing on ABC Saturday mornings in January 1973; America Rock 1975-76; Money Rock introduced in the 1993 revival; added to National Recording Registry 2018.

USCIS 2025 civics test Q12: economic system of the United States: 'Capitalism' or 'Free market economy'; Q11 'Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness' in Declaration; Q73 colonists came for reasons including 'Economic opportunity'.

WSJ/NORC, 10-23 July 2025, n=1,527: 31% say the American dream still holds true, 46% once did but not anymore, 23% never did; 25% believe they have a good chance of improving their standard of living (record low since 1987); 78% not confident their children's generation will be better off.

AP-NORC, 16-20 April 2026, n=2,596: a third say the Dream (if you work hard you'll get ahead) still holds, half say it once did, 15% never; Republicans 57%, independents 24%, Democrats 17%; 60+ 46%, 18-29 22%; White 40%, Black 19%.

ad1_sellers.topic: Who sells the Dream: presidents of both parties, the homeownership push, builders and lenders

claims.text: Clinton, 16 July 1992: 'I was raised to believe the American Dream was built on rewarding hard work'; spoke for those who 'play by the rules'.
Clinton, 17 February 1993: 'if you work 40 hours a week and you've got a child in the house, you will no longer be in poverty' (EITC expansion).

Clinton, 5 June 1995: National Homeownership Strategy aimed to 'boost home ownership to 67.5 percent by the year 2000', up to 8 million families; 100 specific actions; homeownership 'the new way home for the American middle class'.

Bush, 17 June 2002: goal of 5.5 million more minority homeowners by 2010; 'if you own your own home, you're realizing the American Dream'; Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and FHLBs to commit more than $440 billion to minority markets; National Association of Home Builders and Realtors named as partners; American Dream Downpayment Fund to help 40,000 families a year.

Bush, 16 December 2003, signing American Dream Downpayment Act (P.L. 108-186): $200 million a year, at least 40,000 low-income families; homeownership at record 68.4%; 'promote an ownership society in America'.

Obama, 6 December 2011, Osawatomie: 'a make-or-break moment for the middle class'; working people should earn enough to raise a family, build modest savings, own a home, secure their retirement; CEO pay from about 30 to 110 times the worker.
Obama, 28 January 2014 SOTU: 'build new ladders of opportunity into the middle class'; 'Upward mobility has stalled'; 'Opportunity is who we are'.
Trump, 16 June 2015: 'Sadly, the American dream is dead' and he would bring it back bigger and better and stronger than ever.
Trump inaugural, 20 January 2025: 'The golden age of America begins right now'; 'The American Dream will soon be back and thriving like never before.'
Harris, 25 September 2024: 'opportunity economy'; proposed $25,000 down payment assistance for first-time buyers and 3 million new homes and rentals.
Labor Department 'Own Your Own Home' campaign 1918; Hoover's Better Homes in America early 1920s; FHA and VA; mortgage interest deduction kept in 1986.

Own Your Own Home campaign launched by National Association of Real Estate Boards, taken over by the Labor Department in 1917, promotional, no financial incentives; FHA made the 20-30 year amortised 80% mortgage the norm (previously 5-10 years, ~50%); Census homeownership 1920 45.6%, 1940 43.6%, 1960 61.9%; Hoover 1925 quote; 1995 HUD report said benefits 'seldom' tested; ADDI 'almost a purely symbolic gesture'.
Fannie Mae pledged $2 trillion in housing finance to 18 million underserved families over 10 years (American Dream Commitment).

Levittown houses sold at $7,990 advertised as 'the housing buy of the century'; FHA/VA loan packages; 1947 rental contract restricted occupancy to 'members of the Caucasian race'; 1949 salesman told Black veteran builders had not decided to sell to Negroes; 1990 census counted 127 African-Americans.
Ameriquest billed itself as 'sponsor of the American dream'; made at least $80.6bn in high-interest loans 2005-2007; stopped lending August 2007.
Ameriquest settlement 23 January 2006: $325 million with 49 states and DC ($295m restitution); alleged misstated rates and prepayment penalties, inflated incomes, pressured appraisers.
FCIC: 'Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac contributed to the crisis but were not a primary cause'; 'government housing policies were not a significant factor in the crisis'.
Wallison dissent: government housing policy was 'the sine qua non of the financial crisis', producing 27 million subprime and other risky loans.
